1:
Matthew Henry reads the opening as a lesson in communion with God. We must fix his law as our rule, learn it, since we cannot forget what we never knew, and remember it so that it is ready when needed; wills and affections must conform as well as heads, and both tables of the law be deposited in the heart as in the ark of the testimony. The promise attached is long life and prosperity, the commandments adding length of days on earth and eternal life in heaven besides. John Gill reads my law as doctrine, the doctrine of Christ and the truths of the Gospel. John Wesley keeps it the law of God, called his law as the gospel is called Paul’s gospel, because delivered by him.

On the reward they split by degree. Gill observes that the law of Moses promised long life to its observers, while the Gospel brings immortal life to light and promises everlasting life to believers. Adam Clarke counts three eminent blessings, long days, years of lives and peace, glossed as health, long life and abundance. Charles Ellicott presses a distinction: long life means a life worth living, whereas length of days implies only extension, the reward promised for obedience to parents.

Mercy and truth divide them more sharply. Gill takes them as duties, mercy shown by relieving want, by pity and counsel, by forgiving offences and restoring the backslidden, and truth by exercising faith, speaking truth to a neighbour and holding fast the Gospel; but many, he reports, read the clause as a promise instead, that mercy and truth shall not forsake thee, meaning the mercy and truth of God. Ellicott would rather render the pair love and faithfulness, the first shown by God to man and by man to God and his fellow, the second used of both and meaning especially the keeping of promises; they are the attributes by which God is known in his dealings with men, and must therefore be imitated. Wesley divides them by object, mercy covering benignity and charity, faithfulness the duties we owe under the rules of justice.

The binding and writing are read as figures. Ellicott compares them to the figurative orders about keeping the Law whose literal reading produced prayer-fillets and phylacteries, texts enclosed in a leather case and tied at prayer on the arm and forehead; and he corrects table to tablet. Keil and Delitzsch take the neck ornament to be the signet carried on a string rather than a ring, and say the clauses recall the same phylacteries, in which what stands here as figure is given external form, though the real figure is of what is required inwardly; the tablet is one prepared for writing by polish, and to write love and fidelity there is to impress both duties so deeply that a man is impelled to them from within outward. Clarke asks the same in shorter words: let them be constant companions, kept in view, made the moving principles, felt as well as seen. Wesley has them bound like a chain with which people adorn the neck.

The favour promised is read on both sides at once. Gill takes it as grace from God, as Noah found, and as esteem among men, as Joseph had with Potiphar and the keeper of the prison. Clarke makes the first acceptance with God and a sense of his approbation, the second a public verdict: men weigh a character and give credit for sincerity, and though religion is often persecuted where it is not yet known, a benevolent character is generally prized where it is — the envy of men being itself a proof of the excellence of what they envy. Ellicott notes the pairing is particularly used of the childhood of our Lord. Wesley keeps understanding practical, the knowledge of duty and the discerning of good from evil.
5:
John Gill defines the trust by what it excludes: not the best creature nor any creature enjoyment, not riches or strength or wisdom, not descent or education, not a deceitful heart, not works of righteousness, not a profession of religion or its duties, not frames nor graces, not even faith itself, but the Lord only, at all times, in affliction and temptation and darkness. Adam Clarke lays the precept out in steps: God is the fountain of all good, has made his creatures dependent, requires them to be conscious of it, has promised to supply their need, and commands belief without doubt, with the whole heart. Lean not, he adds, means do not prop thyself; he who trusts in his own heart is a fool. Keil and Delitzsch explain why the admonition is interposed here: kindness and truth were commended toward God as well as men, and true prosperity comes from God alone, who knows the right way and what benefits us, and can free us from what harms.

Acknowledging him in all thy ways is taken as a rule of daily conduct. Gill would have a man set the Lord always in view, take no step without his leave, make the Scriptures his counsellors, submit when things go cross and give the glory when they succeed. Clarke asks that every work be begun and ended with God, since we never honour him without serving ourselves; he quotes his old manuscript Bible, have trost in the Lord of all thin herte and ne lene thou to thi prudence, and calls self-sufficiency the ruin of mankind since the fall of Adam, the grand sin of the race being the endeavour to live independently of God.

On being wise in one’s own eyes the tone hardens. Gill describes the conceited man as one who will not consult others and thinks himself wiser than his teachers and than the Scriptures, glorying in an acquisition he does not ascribe to God — and what men are conceited of is generally folly. Matthew Henry makes it a warning: there is no greater enemy to the power of religion and the fear of God than conceitedness of our own wisdom, since those with an opinion of their own sufficiency think it a disparagement to be hampered by religion’s rules; to fear the Lord so as to depart from evil is true wisdom, but self-denyingly so. Charles Ellicott notes only that Job reached the same result in his inquiry after wisdom.

The reward is bodily, and the navel occupies everyone. Gill calls it the knot of the intestines, put for the inward parts and so for the whole body, notes that the Septuagint renders it thy body, and reports a Jewish reading that makes wisdom the subject. Ellicott takes it as the centre and most important part, comparing the epithet given to Delphi, navel of the earth, and renders marrow literally as watering, or refreshing. Keil and Delitzsch trace the word to a root meaning to bind fast, making it properly the umbilical cord, cut at birth, the firm centre with which independent bodily existence begins; they reject the conjecture reading to thy flesh, by which the old versions generalized an expression not to their taste. Clarke builds a whole doctrine on that anatomy: no more delicate meaning than navel need be sought, since it is by the umbilical cord that the unborn child receives all nourishment and nothing by the mouth, and trust in God is as necessary to nourish the soul as the cord is to a child in the womb. Henry keeps it plainer: the prudence, temperance and sobriety religion teaches, with the good government of the appetites, tend not only to the health of the soul but to a good habit of body. Wesley gives the shortest gloss, the navel standing for the body and the marrow for the strength of the bones.
9:
The command is narrowed first. John Gill insists the gift be a man’s own, cites the Septuagint reading out of thy just labours as excluding what is got by fraud, and observes that only a proportionate part is asked. Substance is the mammon of the Targum, which set against heavenly things has no substance in it; men honour God with it by giving to the poor, especially poor saints, by supporting worship, and by communicating to the ministers of the Gospel. Adam Clarke keeps the old gratitude-offering in force without end: a portion of everything by which we get our support belongs to God or to the poor, the representatives of Christ. When that portion is disposed of the rest is sanctified; when it is withheld, the curse is on the whole. John Wesley makes it a rule of expenditure, an estate laid out not to please oneself but to glorify God, the firstfruits being the chief or best.

Keil and Delitzsch are surprised that the wisdom writing, separated from the ceremonial law, should commend tithes; but the consciousness of that duty is older than the law of Moses, so the words stand as a general ethical expression, and the technical terms for tithing never occur in the book. The verb translated honour, they note, means to make heavy, while the noun for wealth means lightness in the sense of opulence, so the phrase is a small paradox. On the promised return they identify the granary and the vat into which the must flows from the press, and compare the same promise in a later prophet, as does Charles Ellicott, who calls the presses vats for newly pressed juice. Gill reads the plenty as bread for the eater and seed for the sower, so that givers are gainers; Wesley says the same in a line, that this is not the way to diminish an estate but to increase it.

Gill thinks the turn to chastening forestalls an objection, since the children of God are often afflicted, pious though they be. That the words are quoted in the New Testament as an exhortation to children settles the address for him: my son is not one person, not a son of Solomon according to the flesh nor a pupil, but all the children of God in every age. Clarke unfolds the word, which carries correction, discipline and instruction together: teaching shows the way, discipline makes it effectual, and correction brings the mind into a submission without which it cannot acquire knowledge. Rebellion is useless; the man who kicks against the pricks wounds his own soul, and since God will either end him or mend him, Clarke asks whether he will kick on.

Ellicott calls the verse a wonderful advance beyond the Pentateuch, where reward and punishment followed immediately on behaviour and misfortune could only be a sign of displeasure; here the Father who sends trouble is no longer an offended parent punishing faults but one who in love corrects, and the New Testament quotes the words with approval, adding nothing. Keil and Delitzsch set the contrast structurally, that as God should not be forgotten in prosperity, so a man should not let adversity estrange him; they translate the noun as school, since the verb means to take one into school, and call the two verses the most suitable motto for the book of Job, the first stating its problem and the second its solution. Wesley marks two ways of failing, making light of the correction or accounting it unnecessary, and growing weary by thinking it tedious, where it should be esteemed a privilege and endured with cheerfulness. Gill and Clarke close on the motive: the chastening springs from love with no abatement of love in it, and Clarke adds that the Septuagint rendering of the last clause, chasteneth every son whom he receiveth, is what the apostle quotes word for word.
13:
Matthew Henry asks what we get by wisdom once found, since the prospect of advantage spurs industry. To find it is first to get it: to draw it from God with the bucket of prayer; to take pains as one draws ore from a mine; to improve in it, making five talents ten; and to do good with it, drawing from the stock as wine from the vessel. John Gill takes wisdom here to be Christ, and finding him to suppose a seeking that arises from grace, not nature. John Wesley says only that finding supposes diligent searching.

The merchandise draws both sides. Gill makes the believer a spiritual merchant and faith a trading with and for Christ, in which a man parts with sinful pleasures, his own righteousness, friends set in competition, and even life; silver is inferior because a man may have abundance of it and lose his soul, and is never satisfied, while he who has Christ has enough. Adam Clarke goes at the word, which means traffic carried on the backs of camels, from a root meaning to go about, and he compares the mines, where a slave won his liberty by finding a diamond of a certain weight, while the finder of wisdom obtains the liberty of the Gospel and is adopted as an heir.

What stone is meant divides the philologists. Keil and Delitzsch argue for corals from the name, built on the idea of shooting forth like a plant, so that it covers a branch and what multiplies branch-like, and from the redness attributed to these elsewhere against the whiteness of snow and milk; they allow the sense may have generalized, pearls being the rendering of later authorities. Charles Ellicott calls the Hebrew doubtful, agrees the colour was red, and thinks coral probable, pearls unlikely. Clarke says the word principally means pearls but may cover precious stones generally, and suggests that a ruby may be named from the cutting that gives it different faces. Gill records the Targum and Septuagint rendering it precious stones, one Latin version as all riches, and points to the gradation from silver to fine gold to jewels.

The two hands are a picture, then a dispute. Gill sees a queen holding length of days where a sceptre would be and riches and honour where the globe would be, and recalls that the king who asked for wisdom got long life and riches with it. Keil and Delitzsch weigh them: length of days is the chief good, belonging in the right, riches and honour the addition, goods which do not condition life but elevate its happiness. Clarke denies the distinction outright: her hands are alike full of the choicest benefits, and nothing is to be understood by the right in preference to the left, though a wicked man shortens his days by excess and a righteous man lengthens his by temperance.

Keil and Delitzsch define the pleasant ways as those on which a man gets what agrees with the inner and outer man, and insist the paths are not paths of peace but peace itself, wisdom bringing well-being on all sides and deep inward satisfaction. Ellicott calls peace the highest reward the New Testament holds out for thankful dependence on God; Wesley makes it a tranquillity of mind and conscience. The tree of life draws every voice back to the garden. Clarke thinks it probable enough that the fruit of that tree might have repaired the wastes of nature continually and prevented death for ever, and says true religion preserves men in life and lets them triumph in death Keil and Delitzsch draw the figure from the history of paradise, and note that the old saying making the cross of Christ the tree of life accommodates itself in a measure here. Wesley calls it a pledge of everlasting life, the only restorer of what we lost by sin.
19:
The turn to creation is read at two pitches. John Gill takes the wisdom by which the earth was founded to be the essential Wisdom of God, the Son, not an instrument but an efficient cause with the Father, and cites a Targum reading by wisdom God created. John Wesley leaves the choice open between Christ and the divine perfection of wisdom that is the fountain of wisdom in man. Charles Ellicott calls the verse anticipatory of a New Testament doctrine, and notes a further advance toward the personality of the Creator later in this book. Adam Clarke takes wisdom in what he calls its proper acceptation, the knowledge and skill manifested in the composition of the earth and the economy of the heavens: God established the order as well as the essence of things, so that though they vary in position they never change place or property.

The breaking up of the depths is disputed philologically. Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading that makes it a division of the waters above the firmament from those below; the verb is used of water bursting forth from the bowels of the earth, and the sense is the overflowing of the ground for cultivation and irrigation, the depths being its inner water stores. The second clause, they add, concerns the waters above. Ellicott renders the verb burst forth and notes that dew matters greatly where for months together there is no rain. Gill takes the depths for fountains and rivers and the cavity that holds the sea. Clarke gathers it into one point: God determined how to break up the fountains of the great deep, appointed the fissures through which springs rise, and exhales and precipitates the vapours — so that the wisest of men ascribes to God the effects we suppose to spring from natural causes.

From that height the writer returns to exhortation. Keil and Delitzsch call the move characteristic, since he speaks of wisdom only with an ethical intention; the things to be kept are wisdom, understanding and knowledge, which belong to God and become the possession of those who aim at them. Matthew Henry asks that religion’s rules be kept always in view and always at heart: a man learning to write keeps his eye on the copy, and the words of wisdom are to be looked at the same way, while the heart is the treasury in which they are stored, this being wealth worth keeping. Gill insists that what is kept in view is not the works done by Wisdom but wisdom itself, one of the names of Christ; Wesley reads the eyes as the eyes of the mind. Clarke draws a creed out of the two nouns: to acknowledge God as the author of all good is the essence of a godly man’s belief, and to resolve to act by his direction is the purpose that follows.

The promised security is described in domestic terms. Henry makes wisdom life to the soul, quickening a man when he begins to be slothful and reviving him when he droops. Gill takes the life to be Christ himself and the Gospel the means of reviving drooping saints, and Wesley glosses the grace to the neck as a beautiful chain or ornament. Keil and Delitzsch say the point is larger, that wisdom makes its possessor confident in God in every situation. Gill spells that out at bedtime: a man who has committed himself to a faithful Creator is not afraid of thieves, of fire consuming his dwelling, or of nocturnal apparitions, nor is he surprised out of sleep or terrified in it by anxious cares and distressing dreams. Clarke observes that most people are afraid of sleep lest they never wake, knowing themselves neither innocent nor pardoned, whereas those who know God is their keeper lie down confident, and their sleep, undisturbed by foreboding and evil dreams, is sweet.
25:
John Gill takes the sudden fear of anything terrible that comes unawares, or of rumours that danger is near, and answers that a man is safe under the care of the keeper of Israel, who neither slumbers nor sleeps. John Wesley explains why the fear is called sudden, unexpected evils being the most frightful, and notes that fear stands for the evils feared. Charles Ellicott glosses the desolation of the wicked as the storm which overwhelms them.

The turn to the neighbour is the sharpest part. Matthew Henry says true wisdom lies in our duty toward man as well as God, in honesty as well as piety, and traces the withholding either to want of love for the poor or to too much love of money. If a man has disabled himself by extravagance that is his great fault; if God has disabled him, his grief should be not that he is straitened in his own comforts but that he has nothing left to give. The excuse of a more convenient season is answered plainly: no one is sure of living until tomorrow. Adam Clarke presses the wording, which he renders from the lords of it, and asks who those owners are. They are the poor; the rich man is a steward given substance that he may divide it, and the poor own every farthing he can spare beyond his own support. Were this a civil case, Clarke says, the law would take him by the throat and lay him up in prison; as it is, God alone judges, and judgment without mercy awaits the man who has shown none.

Ellicott reaches the same duty by another road: we are not absolute owners but stewards of the manifold grace of God, and the friends made by our liberality may welcome us when we fail, that is, die. Wesley widens the good past money to counsel, comfort and reproof, and the recipients to all men by the sovereign law of love; Gill lists honour and tribute to magistrates and payment of debts alongside alms. Clarke adds the reason for haste, that death may take either the giver or the asker before the morrow.

Keil and Delitzsch organize the remaining precepts as illustrations of neighbourly love, harmlessness and then peaceableness. On devising evil they weigh the verb, which means to cut into, used of the smith and the carpenter but just as commonly of ploughing, so the phrase may mean to fabricate evil or to plough it; the old versions divide. Gill takes the ploughing sense, turning up the heart to find evil against a neighbour as the earth is turned by the plough, when a good man should devise good. Wesley notes that the neighbour dwells securely because he relies on your integrity.

On striving Keil and Delitzsch put the rule simply: contending with any man without sufficient reason ought to be abandoned, and no such reason exists where he has done no harm. Gill divides the striving into words, wrangling over trifles, and deeds, lawsuits brought on nothing. Clarke warns against a litigious spirit and too nice a sense of honour: a man who must appeal to judicial authority should avoid enmity and do nothing in revenge, but where no harm has been done, why contend at all, since others might contend with him on the same terms. The last warning turns on envy. Gill describes the oppressor as one who gets wealth by injustice, rapine and violence, and tells the reader not to wish himself in that man’s place, since his end will be bad; Wesley says the envy is of his impunity and success; Keil and Delitzsch make it a warning against fellowship with the loveless. Clarke ends on a harder question: power is bewitching, every man desires it and yet all hate tyrants — but if all had power, would not the greater part be tyrants themselves?
32:
John Gill takes the froward man as one perverse in words and actions, and says he is not merely abominable but an abomination itself. Against him stands the secret of the Lord. Adam Clarke reads that concretely, as a secret assembly where godly people meet and God dwells; Charles Ellicott takes it as confidential intercourse, and reaches for the promise that Father and Son will come and make their abode with the believer. John Wesley concludes that the froward must sooner or later be miserable, while the righteous are God’s friends, to whom he imparts favours other men are strangers to.

Keil and Delitzsch insist that neither curse nor blessing is a matter of goods: the centre of the curse is a disquiet of conscience, and of the blessing the consciousness that God is with us, a rest of soul certain of his grace. Ellicott follows the word for the dwelling further, observing that it often means pasture or sheepfold, a relic of the time before fixed habitations, when the cry to your tents survived long after the settlement in Canaan. Gill keeps the curse legal: the wicked man as a transgressor is under the curse of the law, so his house, his substance and his very blessings are curses, and a plentiful estate may end in penury; one reading makes it the curse of want. Clarke makes the two dwellings a matter of company: no godly people meet in the one house and God is never an inmate there, while he counts the habitation of the just his own temple, worshipped in spirit and in truth. Wesley notes the curse falls on the posterity as well as the person.

The scorner clause has travelled furthest. Gill describes the scorners as those who make a mock at sin and a jest of religion, and notes that the Greek version, which two apostles follow, renders it he resisteth the proud; he cites Jewish writers who explain the scorners as men that will not look upon the divine Being but go on boldly in sin as though there were no God; and since proud men yield to none but resist others, the Greek verb followed. Clarke gives the same Greek line and notes that two apostles quote it exactly as it stands, changing only the divine name. Keil and Delitzsch resist the common rendering that makes the first clause a condition and the second its consequence: the one fact is not the consequence but the reverse of the other, and the connecting word in such antitheses generally means on the other hand; several old versions pass over the particle, and one translator makes it an asseveration, which they deny it can bear. Ellicott renders it although he scorns the scorners, yet to the lowly he giveth grace, another form of the earlier teaching that offers of mercy rejected are in time withdrawn, so that as a man deals with God, God will at last deal with him.

Gill identifies the wise with the just and lowly already named, and defines the wisdom as neither natural nor civil nor merely notional but a wisdom unto salvation, in which a man knows the sinfulness of his nature and his want of a righteousness to justify him. Clarke grounds the inheritance in family: the wise man is a child of the heavenly household with heaven for his portion, while fools have ignominy for their exaltation, many of them exalted to the gibbet and gallows. Keil and Delitzsch dispute the last verb, refusing the rendering that shame sweeps fools away, since the word means to raise something high; better that shame exalts them, who owe their celebrity to it as warning examples. Ellicott ends on the same note, that dull people who despise the threatenings are distinguished by what is a disgrace to them, and are noticeable only as examples to be shunned.
